National

and I

or
two transects are pseudo replicas not replicas. I saw more experienced
investigators use 1, 2 or 3 transects, I read Buckland=92s book, and =
they
don=92t say the minimum amount of transects we should use. I=92m almost =
sure 2
transects are good enough but I don=92t know how to argue that it is =
valid. Or
maybe is not? And also about the pseudo replicas.
3. Another thing that I would like to do with these data, it is to
compare it with data given by Dr. Louise Emmons (1984), I know the
methodology that she used was the line transect census, but she measured =
the
perpendicular distance from the first animal of the cluster and I =
measured
it from the animal in the center of the cluster. Do you think I can =
compare
them?

=20

=20

Maybe, these questions are a bit out of the questions I should ask to =
the
list, but it is very hard to look for an advice here in Peru.=20

=20

Thanks for your time,=20

=20

Natalia

messages.author: 4b4a7b00c1dd09c7
messages.subject: Re: Primate census
parts:
Hi Natalia, list:

There are several problems with your design.

Firstly, you surveyed from established tracks. This raises two issues. (i)
density along tracks is unlikely to be the same as average density in the
whole national park, so you can only make inferences about density in the
area you survyved, not the whole park; (ii) if density of animals is
affected by distance from track (e.g., they use the tracks) then the
assumption used in estimating the detection function that true density is
uniform with respect to perpendicular distance is incorrect, so you get a
biased estimate of detection probability and so a biased estimate of
density, even along the tracks. You should locate transects at random
(preferrably systematic random) throughout the study area of interest and if
you must cut the lines use minimal cutting. See chapter 7 of the
Introduction to Distance Sampling book for lots more on this (particuarly
sections 7.8.3 on repeat transects, 7.8.4 on cut transects and 7.8.5 on the
use of paths).

Secondly you only surveyed 2 transects. This is not enough to give you a
reliable estimate of the spatial variation in density, which is usually a
major component of the overall variance estimate. So, the CVs you have
obtained are very unrealiable. When you survey the same line many times,
you should pool all detections from the same lines together at the analysis
stage (and multiply line length by the number of visits) - you then have a
sample size of 2 transects for estimating variation in encounter rate
between transects, not 24. This has been covered a few times in previous
posts to this list (check the archives, which are searchable). You probably
missed the bit in the book about recommended minimum sample size of
transects - in section 7.2.1 they recommend 10-20, and I'd go for 20 over
10!

You asked about comparing the results with those of someone who measured
perpendicular distance to the first animal of the cluster rather than the
center. You did the correct thing (see pages 119 and 272 of the book);
their method will produce an upward bias in the density estimate.

In my experience, there is a great deal of poor practice in both field and
analysis methods in the primate survey literature. I don't know why this
is, but you certainly need to be careful when comparing your results to
those of others.

I hope this helps,

- Len
